title: More Equations than Unknowns, and Fewer
quickIdea: Counting equations against unknowns decides nothing. m greater than n can still be consistent and m less than n can still be inconsistent; only the ranks settle it, with one exception that does follow from counting.
remember: m > n does not force inconsistency: redundant equations can be dropped, and a consistent overdetermined system has exactly one solution when rank(A) = n.
m < n does not guarantee a solution for a non-homogeneous system: x + y + z = 1 and x + y + z = 2 has two equations, three unknowns and no solution.
m < n does guarantee a non-trivial solution of the homogeneous system Ax = 0, because rank(A) is at most m < n.
m = n guarantees nothing by itself, but it does guarantee that some system with that A has a solution, namely the consistent ones; a unique solution needs rank(A) = n.
A useful sufficient condition: if rank(A) = m, the number of rows, then every b is reachable and the system is consistent for all b.

example.prompt: For systems of m linear equations in n variables, which of these is correct: (I) m < n implies all such systems have a solution; (II) m > n implies none has a solution; (III) m = n implies there exists a system which has a solution?
example.work: I fails: x + y + z = 1 and x + y + z = 2 has m = 2 < n = 3 and no solution. II fails: x + y = 1, 2x + 2y = 2, x - y = 0 has m = 3 > n = 2, and x = y = 1/2 satisfies all three equations, so a system with more equations than unknowns can be consistent. III holds: take m = n = 1 and the equation x = 0.
example.answer: Only III is true. This is GATE CSE 2016 Set 2 Q.04, whose correct option is 'Only III is true'.

gateAngle: GATE CSE 2016 Set 2 Q.04 is exactly this card. GATE CSE 2024 Set 1 Q.39 runs the same idea for a wide matrix and asks what the nullity is guaranteed to be, and GATE CSE 1996 Q.1.7 tests the m < n homogeneous guarantee.

variations.label: ORIGINAL PYQ-STYLE QUESTION
variations.question: Give a system with more equations than unknowns that has infinitely many solutions.
variations.why: Three equations, two unknowns, all three the same line: rank(A) = rank([A|b]) = 1 < 2, so there are infinitely many solutions despite m > n.

variations.label: CONCEPTUAL PRACTICE QUESTION
variations.question: If rank(A) equals the number of rows of A, why is Ax = b consistent for every b?
variations.answer: Because the columns of A then span the whole of R^m, so every b is a combination of them.
variations.why: rank([A|b]) has the same number of rows as A, so it cannot exceed m; since rank(A) = m already, the two ranks are equal for every b.

trap.what: Answering a 'which statement is true' question about m and n by intuition about 'too many equations' or 'too few equations'.
trap.why: The counts m and n bound the rank but do not fix it. The only safe conclusions are the ones the rank inequality gives, such as nullity at least m - n for a wide matrix.
trap.counterexample: x + y + z = 1 and x + y + z = 2 has fewer equations than unknowns and is inconsistent, so 'fewer equations means solvable' is false.

check.question: A is 5 x 3 with rank 3. Is Ax = b consistent for every b in R^5?
check.explanation: rank(A) = 3 is less than the number of rows 5, so the columns span only a 3-dimensional subspace of R^5 and most b are unreachable. Consistency for all b needs rank(A) = m.
